topic: Day 1 · Acute Tubular Necrosis, Contrast & Pigment Nephropathy
speakerBio: Nephrologist who runs the trauma-and-toxins renal service and has made a small crusade of retiring the bicarbonate-and-mannitol rituals in favour of the evidence: isotonic fluid and high tubular flow.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

A 24-year-old man is brought in after being found collapsed on his bathroom floor, having lain there for an unknown number of hours after a night out. He is agitated, his urine in the catheter bag is the colour of cola, and his first bloods show a creatinine of 240 µmol/L, a potassium of 6.1, and a creatine kinase of 48,000 U/L. The FY1, remembering something about myoglobin, asks whether they should "alkalinise the urine with bicarbonate and give mannitol." Stop — because two of the three things this patient most needs are simple, and one of the things he is about to be given may be a myth that harms him. This session is about the kidney's most common intrinsic injury, acute tubular necrosis, and its three great precipitants — ischaemia, contrast, and pigment — where the mechanisms are elegant, the prevention is mostly just salt and water, and several cherished 'renoprotective' rituals have been quietly killed by good trials.

1 · 🔬 Acute tubular necrosis — the anatomy of a dying tubule

ATN is the structural sequel to the pre-renal state: when hypoperfusion or a toxin overwhelms the tubular cell — above all the oxygen-starved S3 segment of the proximal tubule and the medullary thick ascending limb (the outer-medullary watershed from session 1) — the cell suffers ATP depletion and a cascade of injury. Four mechanistic events explain the entire clinical picture:

MechanismWhat happensClinical consequence
Loss of tubular polarityATP depletion disrupts the cytoskeleton; Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and integrins mislocate from the basolateral membrane to the apical surfaceTubule stops vectorial sodium reabsorption → high FeNa; cells lose their grip on the basement membrane
Cell detachment & cast formationViable and dead cells slough into the lumen and clump with Tamm-Horsfall proteinMuddy-brown granular casts; intratubular obstruction raising PBS and dropping GFR
Back-leak of filtrateDenuded, leaky epithelium lets glomerular filtrate leak back across into the interstitiumEffective GFR falls further — filtrate never reaches the bladder
The extension phaseReperfusion brings inflammation, microvascular congestion and reactive oxygen species that injure more cells even after the initial insult is overInjury deepens for days after the blood pressure is fixed — why ATN doesn't reverse instantly

The extension phase is the concept that surprises people: fixing the haemodynamics does not switch ATN off, because reperfusion itself drives a second wave of inflammatory and oxidative injury and the outer-medullary microvasculature stays congested. This is precisely why an established ATN needs days to weeks to recover through the maintenance and recovery phases, while a pre-renal kidney recovers in hours.

Loss of polarity, casts, back-leak, extension phase — four mechanisms, and every one of them means an ATN kidney cannot simply be 'refilled' back to health like a pre-renal one.
💡 The muddy-brown granular cast

The pathognomonic urinary finding of ATN is the muddy-brown (pigmented) granular cast — sloughed tubular epithelial cells and debris trapped in a Tamm-Horsfall protein matrix. Seeing them on microscopy of a fresh, spun urine effectively confirms established ATN and, with a FeNa >2%, pulls you decisively away from a pre-renal diagnosis. Ask the lab to look, or look yourself.

ATN causes split into ischaemic (prolonged hypoperfusion, shock, sepsis, cardiac arrest, major surgery) and nephrotoxic (aminoglycosides, amphotericin, cisplatin, and the three pigment/crystal syndromes below). The mechanisms overlap: both funnel into the ATP-depleted, polarity-losing S3 cell.

2 · 🩻 Contrast-associated AKI — mechanism and the collapse of a diagnosis

Iodinated contrast can injure the kidney by two mechanisms acting together: direct tubular toxicity (contrast is directly cytotoxic to tubular epithelium and generates reactive oxygen species) and medullary ischaemia (contrast triggers renal vasoconstriction, worsening the oxygen supply of the already-vulnerable outer medulla). Classically the creatinine rises at 48–72 hours and recovers over 1–2 weeks.

But the modern story is one of humility. Much of what was historically called "contrast-induced nephropathy" was really the background AKI that sick, comorbid patients develop anyway — and rigorous propensity-matched and controlled data show that with modern low-osmolar contrast the truly attributable risk is far smaller than feared. The terminology has shifted accordingly to contrast-associated AKI (CA-AKI) — associated, not necessarily caused.

Who is actually at riskWho is largely not
Pre-existing significant CKD (eGFR <30, and the higher-risk end of 30–44)Normal baseline renal function
Diabetic nephropathyWell-hydrated, euvolaemic patients
Hypovolaemia / hypotension at the time of the scanModern low-osmolar/iso-osmolar, modest-volume contrast
Large contrast loads, intra-arterial administration, concurrent nephrotoxins

Prevention — volume, and only volume

The one intervention with a coherent mechanism and supportive evidence is peri-procedural volume expansion with intravenous isotonic saline in at-risk patients — expanding the effective circulating volume, preserving medullary perfusion and diluting the tubular contrast load.

⚠️ The death of 'renoprotective' bicarbonate and N-acetylcysteine

For years, at-risk patients received intravenous sodium bicarbonate (to scavenge reactive oxygen species by alkalinising the medulla) and oral N-acetylcysteine (as an antioxidant). The PRESERVE trial (Weisbord et al., NEJM 2018), a large 2×2 factorial RCT in high-risk patients undergoing angiography, showed no benefit of bicarbonate over saline, and no benefit of N-acetylcysteine over placebo for any renal or clinical endpoint. The AMACING trial (Nijssen et al., Lancet 2017) went further, showing that in most at-risk patients no prophylactic hydration was non-inferior to hydration — and that the hydration itself caused harm (fluid overload) in some. Bottom line: give isotonic saline to genuinely high-risk patients, do not give bicarbonate or NAC, and never delay an urgent, indicated scan out of exaggerated contrast fear.

For contrast, the only proven prophylaxis is salt and water in the genuinely at-risk. Bicarbonate and N-acetylcysteine are dead — PRESERVE and AMACING buried them.

3 · 💪 Rhabdomyolysis and pigment nephropathy — myoglobin as a tubular poison

When skeletal muscle breaks down en masse — crush injury, prolonged immobility ("long lie"), seizures, extreme exertion, statins, the serotonin/neuroleptic-malignant syndromes, drugs and toxins — it dumps myoglobin, potassium, phosphate and creatine kinase into the circulation. Myoglobin is directly nephrotoxic by three converging mechanisms:

  1. Tubular obstruction — myoglobin precipitates with Tamm-Horsfall protein, especially in acidic urine, forming pigmented casts that block the tubule.
  2. Direct tubular cytotoxicity — the haem iron catalyses reactive-oxygen-species-mediated (Fenton) injury to tubular cells.
  3. Renal vasoconstriction — myoglobin scavenges nitric oxide, causing renal vasoconstriction and worsening medullary ischaemia.

Add the volume depletion of third-spacing into injured muscle, and you have a perfect ATN-generating storm.

The numbers

  • CK is the diagnostic and prognostic marker. AKI risk rises with CK, becoming clinically important above roughly 5,000 U/L and substantial above 15,000–20,000 U/L; the very high values (tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands) carry the greatest risk.
  • Urine dipstick positive for blood but few/no red cells on microscopy = the classic clue, because the dipstick detects the haem of myoglobin, not intact RBCs.
  • Watch for hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hypocalcaemia (calcium deposits in injured muscle) and, later, rebound hypercalcaemia.

Treatment — the cornerstone is aggressive fluid

The single proven intervention is early, aggressive intravenous isotonic fluid resuscitation — often several litres in the first hours, titrated to a brisk urine output (a common target is ~200–300 mL/h) — to restore renal perfusion, flush the tubules, and dilute the myoglobin load before casts form.

⚠️ The myth of bicarbonate and mannitol in rhabdomyolysis

Generations were taught to alkalinise the urine with sodium bicarbonate (theory: reduce myoglobin cast formation and haem toxicity in acidic urine) and to add mannitol (theory: osmotic diuresis to flush casts, plus free-radical scavenging). Neither has ever been shown in controlled human data to be superior to aggressive saline alone, and both carry real harm: bicarbonate causes a metabolic alkalosis that worsens the hypocalcaemia (precipitating tetany) and can promote calcium-phosphate deposition, while mannitol can itself cause an osmotic nephrosis and volume problems and is contraindicated once the patient is anuric. The evidence-based message is blunt: fluids, fluids, fluids — isotonic saline titrated to urine output — and skip the bicarbonate and mannitol rituals. Reserve alkalinisation, if used at all, for specialist-directed selected severe cases, never as a reflex.

Rhabdo is treated with a firehose of saline, not a chemistry set. Bicarbonate and mannitol are unproven and can harm — flow rate beats pH.
💡 Dipstick 'blood', no red cells

A urine dipstick strongly positive for blood with no red cells on microscopy is the fingerprint of a pigment: myoglobin (rhabdomyolysis) or free haemoglobin (intravascular haemolysis). The dipstick's peroxidase reaction detects the haem group, which both pigments carry, but there are no intact erythrocytes to see. Check a CK and an LDH/haptoglobin to tell them apart.

4 · 🧊 Crystal nephropathies — a teaser for tumour lysis

The final mechanism of intrinsic tubular AKI is intratubular crystal deposition, where a solute precipitates within the tubular lumen and obstructs it — mechanistically a cousin of pigment cast nephropathy. The archetype, covered fully in its own session, is tumour lysis syndrome: the massive lysis of a bulky, chemo-sensitive tumour releases a flood of intracellular contents, and two of them crystallise in the tubule:

  • Uric acid (from purine/nucleic-acid breakdown) precipitates in the acidic distal tubule → acute uric acid nephropathy.
  • Calcium phosphate (from the huge phosphate release) precipitates when the calcium-phosphate product is high, especially if the urine has been over-alkalinised.

The prevention logic — aggressive hydration to maintain high tubular flow, plus rasburicase to dissolve the urate load — is again fundamentally about volume and flushing the tubule, echoing everything in this session. And note the elegant contradiction it sets up with old rhabdomyolysis teaching: you would not alkalinise urine in tumour lysis, because although alkali helps urate stay soluble, it drives calcium phosphate out of solution. The full story waits for the tumour-lysis session.

🎯 The unifying thread of intrinsic ATN

Ischaemia, contrast, pigment and crystal all injure the same vulnerable outer-medullary tubule, and — crush injury aside — the same humble intervention dominates prevention and treatment across all of them: restore and maintain effective circulating volume and high tubular flow with isotonic fluid. The fancy adjuncts (bicarbonate, NAC, mannitol) have mostly been retired by trials. Volume is the therapy that keeps winning.

☠️ M&M — the chemistry set that caused a seizure

A 24-year-old man was admitted after a 'long lie' with cola-coloured urine, a creatinine of 240, potassium 6.1 and a CK of 48,000. He was correctly given fluids — but the covering team, working from a decade-old memory of a nephrology tutorial, also started a sodium bicarbonate infusion to alkalinise the urine and a bolus of mannitol, and then, reassured by the 'renoprotective' regimen, ran the saline conservatively to 'avoid overload'. Over the next hours he developed carpopedal spasm and then a generalised seizure. What happened: rhabdomyolysis had already driven his calcium into injured muscle (hypocalcaemia); the bicarbonate-induced metabolic alkalosis sharply worsened the ionised hypocalcaemia, tipping him into symptomatic tetany and a seizure, while the mannitol added an osmotic diuresis that his under-resuscitated circulation could not tolerate. The one thing that actually treats rhabdomyolysis — a firehose of isotonic saline titrated to a urine output of 200–300 mL/h — had been throttled in favour of two unproven adjuncts that harmed him. Lessons: in rhabdomyolysis the evidence supports aggressive isotonic fluid alone; bicarbonate and mannitol are unproven and carry real harm (alkalosis worsening hypocalcaemia; osmotic nephrosis/overload); never let a 'renoprotective' ritual crowd out the resuscitation that is the actual treatment. Flow rate beats pH.

5 · 🎯 Take-home messages

  1. ATN has four mechanisms — loss of tubular polarity (→ high FeNa), cast formation and intratubular obstruction, back-leak of filtrate, and the extension phase of reperfusion injury that makes recovery take days-to-weeks, not hours.
  2. The muddy-brown granular cast plus a FeNa >2% confirms established ATN and rules out a purely pre-renal picture.
  3. Contrast-associated AKI injures via direct tubular toxicity and medullary vasoconstriction, but its attributable risk is much smaller than once believed; real risk concentrates in CKD, diabetes and hypovolaemia.
  4. For contrast, isotonic saline in genuinely high-risk patients is the only proven prophylaxis — PRESERVE killed bicarbonate and N-acetylcysteine, AMACING showed hydration itself can be skipped/harmful in the low-risk; never delay an urgent indicated scan.
  5. Rhabdomyolysis injures the kidney by tubular obstruction (myoglobin casts), direct haem-iron cytotoxicity and NO-scavenging vasoconstriction; CK matters (risk climbs >5,000 and is substantial >15,000–20,000 U/L), and 'dipstick blood, no red cells' is the clue.
  6. Treat rhabdomyolysis with early aggressive isotonic fluid titrated to urine output (~200–300 mL/h); bicarbonate and mannitol are unproven and can harm (alkalosis worsening hypocalcaemia; osmotic nephrosis) — flow beats pH.
  7. Crystal nephropathy (tumour lysis) obstructs the tubule with uric acid and calcium phosphate; prevention is again hydration/high flow plus rasburicase — and, unlike old rhabdo teaching, you do not alkalinise, because that precipitates calcium phosphate.

moderatorQs.q: Describe the four mechanisms by which acute tubular necrosis lowers GFR, and explain why an ATN kidney does not recover as quickly as a pre-renal one.
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Four events in the injured tubule drop the GFR. Loss of tubular polarity: ATP depletion mislocates Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and integrins from the basolateral to the apical membrane, so vectorial sodium reabsorption fails (giving the high FeNa) and cells lose adhesion. Cast formation and intratubular obstruction: sloughed cells clump with Tamm-Horsfall protein into muddy-brown casts that physically block the tubule, raising Bowman's-space pressure and opposing filtration. Back-leak: the denuded, leaky epithelium lets glomerular filtrate diffuse back into the interstitium, so effective clearance falls further. And the extension phase: on reperfusion, inflammation, microvascular congestion and reactive oxygen species injure more cells even after the initial insult resolves. That last mechanism is exactly why an ATN kidney needs days-to-weeks through maintenance and recovery phases — restoring haemodynamics does not undo the structural damage or halt the reperfusion-driven second wave — whereas a pre-renal kidney, being structurally intact, recovers within hours of re-perfusion.

moderatorQs.q: What did the PRESERVE and AMACING trials establish about the prevention of contrast-associated AKI?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Together they dismantled the old prophylaxis rituals. PRESERVE (Weisbord, NEJM 2018), a large 2×2 factorial RCT in high-risk patients undergoing angiography, found no benefit of intravenous sodium bicarbonate over isotonic saline, and no benefit of oral N-acetylcysteine over placebo on any renal or clinical outcome — retiring both agents. AMACING (Nijssen, Lancet 2017) showed that in most at-risk patients withholding prophylactic hydration was non-inferior to giving it, and that the hydration itself caused harm (fluid overload) in some. The distilled message: the only rational prophylaxis is isotonic saline reserved for genuinely high-risk patients (significant CKD, diabetic nephropathy, hypovolaemia, large intra-arterial loads); bicarbonate and NAC are dead; and one must weigh even saline against the harm of overload — and never delay an urgent, clinically indicated contrast scan out of exaggerated fear.

moderatorQs.q: A patient has a CK of 48,000 and cola-coloured urine. What is the cornerstone of treatment, and why are bicarbonate and mannitol discouraged?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: The cornerstone is early, aggressive intravenous isotonic fluid resuscitation — frequently several litres up front and then titrated to a brisk urine output (commonly ~200–300 mL/h) — to restore renal perfusion, maintain high tubular flow, and dilute and flush the myoglobin before it precipitates into obstructing casts. Bicarbonate and mannitol are discouraged because neither has been shown in controlled human data to beat aggressive saline alone, and both carry real harm. Bicarbonate produces a metabolic alkalosis that worsens the hypocalcaemia of rhabdomyolysis (risking tetany and seizures) and can promote calcium-phosphate deposition; mannitol can cause osmotic nephrosis and volume derangement and is contraindicated once the patient is anuric. So the evidence-based approach is fluids titrated to urine output, correct the hyperkalaemia, and abandon the bicarbonate-and-mannitol reflex — flow rate beats pH.

audienceQs.q: The urine dipstick is strongly positive for blood but microscopy shows no red cells. What does that mean?
audienceQs.answerHTML: It means the dipstick is detecting a haem pigment, not intact red cells. The dipstick's peroxidase reaction reacts to the haem group, which is present in myoglobin (from rhabdomyolysis) and free haemoglobin (from intravascular haemolysis) just as it is in red-cell haemoglobin — but in those cases there are no erythrocytes to see under the microscope. In your collapsed patient with cola-coloured urine this points squarely to myoglobinuria from rhabdomyolysis; confirm with a markedly elevated creatine kinase, and check potassium, phosphate and calcium. If instead it were haemolysis you'd expect a low haptoglobin, raised LDH and unconjugated bilirubin. Either way, the discrepancy between dipstick and microscopy is the diagnostic clue.

audienceQs.q: My patient needs an urgent contrast CT to exclude a bleed but has an eGFR of 35. Do I need to delay for prophylaxis?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Do not delay a genuinely urgent, clinically indicated scan — the risk of missing the bleed vastly outweighs the modest, and probably overstated, attributable risk of contrast-associated AKI. An eGFR of 35 places them at the milder end of 'at-risk', so the sensible, evidence-based step is peri-procedural intravenous isotonic saline if time and haemodynamics allow, while ensuring they are euvolaemic and any concurrent nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, etc.) are held. Do not give sodium bicarbonate or N-acetylcysteine — PRESERVE showed neither helps. Proceed with the scan, use the smallest adequate contrast volume, and recheck renal function afterwards. The old practice of delaying urgent imaging for elaborate 'renoprotection' has been abandoned.

audienceQs.q: In severe rhabdomyolysis, how do I titrate the fluids and what electrolyte trap should I watch for?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Resuscitate early and aggressively with isotonic crystalloid — often several litres in the first hours in a young patient with normal cardiac function — and then titrate to urine output, aiming for a brisk flow around 200–300 mL/h, with close monitoring of fluid balance so you flush the tubules without tipping a compromised heart into overload. The key electrolyte traps: hyperkalaemia (from muscle breakdown, often the acute killer — treat it) and hypocalcaemia (calcium sequestered into injured muscle). Do not reflexively give calcium for the hypocalcaemia unless it is symptomatic or there is dangerous hyperkalaemia, because calcium can deposit in injured muscle and there is often a rebound hypercalcaemia in the recovery phase. And avoid the bicarbonate/mannitol rituals — bicarbonate-induced alkalosis will worsen the ionised hypocalcaemia. Fluids titrated to output, treat the potassium, watch the calcium.
